source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning
finding: Of 20+ open reasoning models strong on math, most did not carry the gain to other reasoning or to non-reasoning tasks. The fine-tuning method predicted transfer: RL-tuned models transferred, SFT-tuned ones often lost general skill.
numbers: Defines a Transferability Index (gain on other domain / gain on math, z-normalised, difficulty weighted). Benchmarks: math (AIME24/25, MATH500, OlympiadBench), other reasoning (GPQA-D, LiveCodeBench, ACPBench, HeadQA), non-reasoning (CoQA, MC-TACO, IFEval, HaluEval).
quote: Surprisingly, most models that succeed in math fail to transfer their gains to other domains.
limits: Open-weight models; gains measured against each base model; the index is a ratio so it blows up when the math gain is small.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of the McPeck/Ennis question. Skill learned in one domain does not automatically carry; do not assume a lesson learned on one problem class helps another.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning (controlled Qwen3-14B run)
finding: Controlled test on one base model with math-only data. RL (GRPO) gave gains on other reasoning and on non-reasoning tasks; SFT on teacher traces hurt non-reasoning tasks badly.
numbers: Non-reasoning average (CoQA, MC-TACO, IFEval, HaluEval): base 45.7, SFT-think 21.1, SFT-no-think 29.0, RL 53.2 (RL minus best SFT +24.0). Other-reasoning average: base 30.2, SFT-think 45.3, SFT-no-think 45.2, RL 60.0. Math average: SFT-think 49.8, RL 53.8 (base 27.7). IFEval 69.2 base to 42.3 SFT-think vs 70.0 RL.
limits: One model family (Qwen3-14B-Base), one math dataset, single run per condition as shown. Table was read from PDF text with some column garbling.
agent_relevance: Training-free scaffold keeps weights fixed, so it avoids SFT forgetting; but the same training signal can transfer or not depending on how it was applied. Treat any stored lesson as a hypothesis for other classes.

source: Huan et al. (2025) Does Math Reasoning Improve General LLM Capabilities? Understanding Transferability of LLM Reasoning (mechanism)
finding: SFT shifted hidden-state geometry (PCA) and token distributions (KL) a lot, especially on non-reasoning inputs. RL kept them close to the base. Ablation: sampling distribution, credit assignment and negative gradient helped transfer.
numbers: Qualitative from PCA and KL analyses; KL regularisation judged to play a subtle role.
limits: Explanations are correlational; no human-style transfer test.
agent_relevance: Learning from failed attempts (negative signal) is what generalised; supports keeping failures in lesson memory, not only successes.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
finding: 11 tasks, each with a default form and a counterfactual form needing the same abstract procedure (base-9 arithmetic, 1-based indexing, reordered syntax, altered chess rules, shifted guitar tuning, etc.). GPT-4 and others did above chance on counterfactuals but fell substantially and consistently below default.
numbers: Figure 1: GPT-4 with 0-shot CoT is lower on the counterfactual version for every task pair shown. Counterfactual-comprehension checks (CCC) were mostly passed, so the failure is not just misreading the prompt. Default accuracy tracks how common the default form is in pretraining.
quote: performance substantially and consistently degrades compared to the default conditions
limits: Zero-shot CoT only eases the gap, does not close it. Exact per-task percentages not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Models carry a procedure only partly; they also use narrow default-condition habits. Lessons should record the class conditions (base, order, rule set) under which they were learned.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Re-instantiating GSM8K templates with new names and numbers makes tested models score lower and vary widely. Changing only names barely matters; changing numbers hurts more; adding clauses hurts more still.
numbers: 50 sets of GSM-Symbolic. Gemma2-9B best-to-worst set gap over 12 points. GSM8K score sat on the right tail of the GSM-Symbolic distribution for 21 of 25 models (possible contamination). Gemma2-9B, Phi-3, Phi-3.5, Mathstral-7B dropped more; Llama3-8B and GPT-4o dropped little.
limits: Contamination reading is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Same problem, new surface values: a lesson keyed to exact numbers fails; key lessons to structure, not surface.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic (GSM-NoOp)
finding: Adding one plausible but irrelevant clause (GSM-NoOp) caused a large drop in every model. Models often turned irrelevant statements into operations (for example read 'discount' as multiply). More clauses cut accuracy faster as difficulty rose.
numbers: GSM-NoOp drops up to 65% (Phi-3-mini over 64 points); o1-mini -29.1 points; o1-preview also dropped sharply. Switching the 8-shot examples did not repair it.
limits: 8-shot CoT; authors read this as pattern matching, others dispute that reading.
agent_relevance: A step that checks which facts are needed before computing would target this failure; a transfer test for the agent should include irrelevant-clause variants.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: GSM-IC (GSM8K with one irrelevant sentence) lowers accuracy for CoT, zero-shot CoT, least-to-most and program prompting. Fixes helped but did not remove the problem.
numbers: Fewer than 30% of base problems were solved consistently after distractors (macro accuracy). Least-to-most was the most robust (about double the macro accuracy of CoT with code-davinci-002); exemplars with distractors and an 'ignore irrelevant information' instruction gave notable gains. No drop on plain GSM8K from those fixes.
limits: Codex and text-davinci-003 era; modern models improved but see GSM-NoOp (2024) for the same failure.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level scaffolds (decompose first, tell model to ignore) raise robustness at near-zero cost.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Reordering the premises of a deductive problem, without changing the answer, lowers accuracy. Forward order (matching proof order) is best.
numbers: GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L lost up to 20-30 points; Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo went from over 65% to below 25% (drop over 40 points). R-GSM (reordered GSM8K) also lower for all models. Drop grows with number of rules.
limits: Modus ponens logic tasks plus R-GSM subset; humans not tested here.
agent_relevance: Surface order is a transfer axis. Having the program restate or reorder the problem into a canonical form before solving is a cheap guard.

source: McCoy et al. (2023) Embers of Autoregression: Understanding Large Language Models Through the Problem They are Trained to Solve
finding: LLMs do worse on rare task versions and on low-probability outputs, even when the abstract task is identical. Same skill, different familiarity, different accuracy.
numbers: Word reversal: GPT-4 97% when the answer is a high-probability sentence vs 53% when low-probability. Rot-13 (common cipher): 21% vs 11% for high- vs low-probability input. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 both do much better on common rot-13 than on rare rot-2, though equal in difficulty.
limits: Probability effects shrink with scale and CoT in some cases but did not vanish in tested models.
agent_relevance: Transfer fails along a familiarity axis, not only a domain axis. Class keys for lessons should include how standard the task form is.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Is Chain-of-Thought Reasoning of LLMs a Mirage? A Data Distribution Lens
finding: In a clean train-from-scratch sandbox (DataAlchemy: letter strings plus ROT and shift transforms), chain-of-thought works only when test items match training on task, length and format. Shifts collapse it.
numbers: Exact match 100.00% in-distribution; 0.01% on composition shift, 0% for partially-OOD and fully-OOD in the transformation test. A small amount of SFT on unseen data patched it quickly. Length and format shifts degraded more smoothly. Hundreds of models, 62K to 14B parameters; repeated with LLaMA3-8B and Qwen3-14B fine-tunes.
quote: reflects a structured inductive bias learned from in-distribution data
limits: Small synthetic models; the link to real LLMs is by fine-tuning two real models; pretraining data is opaque.
agent_relevance: A strict view of transfer: reasoning chains reproduce training patterns. Verify any carried-over lesson on the new class before trusting it.

source: Ma et al. (2025) General-Reasoner: Advancing LLM Reasoning Across All Domains
finding: Zero-RL on a broad multi-domain verifiable dataset (WebInstruct-verified) beat math-only RL on general benchmarks. Domain diversity in training aided breadth.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Base: MMLU-Pro 58.9% vs base 47.7% and instruct 57.0%. Math-only training gave +1 point on math (49.1 vs 48.5) but cost about 2 points each on MMLU-Pro, GPQA, SuperGPQA vs full data. At 14B, the full-data model beat math-only on every metric.
limits: Authors' own comparison; technical report.
agent_relevance: Mixed-domain exposure transfers better than single-domain; a lesson store should span several classes, not one narrow one.

source: Suzgun et al. (2025) Dynamic Cheatsheet: Test-Time Learning with Adaptive Memory
finding: A persistent, curated memory of strategies and snippets lifted accuracy at inference with no weight change. Gains were biggest where later questions shared structure with earlier ones.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet AIME 2024 23.3% to 50.0% (DC-Cu) and AIME 2025 6.7% to 36.7%. GPQA-Diamond 59.6% to 68.7% with retrieval and synthesis (DC-RS). Full-history baseline on AIME 2024 only 26.7%. GPT-4o on Game of 24: 10% baseline, far higher once a solution was found and reused.
limits: Smaller models (Haiku, GPT-4o-mini) gained little or slightly lost; benefit depends on related items in the stream; authors suggest ordering related questions early.
agent_relevance: Direct support for lessons keyed to class: memory helps most inside a class, and curated notes beat raw history (26.7 vs 50.0).

source: Ouyang et al. (2026) ReasoningBank: Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory
finding: Distils reusable strategies from both successful and failed trajectories into a memory. Helps on WebArena, Mind2Web and SWE-Bench-Verified; gain is largest in the hardest cross-domain split.
numbers: WebArena overall success +8.3, +7.2, +4.6 over no memory across three backbones; on the Multi (cross-site) subset +4.6 over best baseline while AWM gave no gain or a loss. Mind2Web cross-domain (Gemini-2.5-flash): step success 31.9 (no memory) to 36.6; element accuracy 35.8 to 40.6; AWM 33.3 element accuracy (below no memory).
limits: Success labels from an LLM judge; Mind2Web task success is low in absolute terms (about 1-5%).
agent_relevance: Failure-derived lessons written abstractly transferred better than success-only workflows. Lesson memory can hurt (AWM below baseline cross-domain).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induced reusable workflows from past tasks help web agents. Online induction (from test queries) generalises better than offline as the train-test gap widens.
numbers: Relative success +24.6% on Mind2Web, +51.1% on WebArena; gap over baselines grows from 8.9 to 14.0 absolute points across cross-task, cross-website, cross-domain. Table 4 (GPT-4): cross-domain step SR 18.6 (MindAct) vs 32.6 offline and 35.5 online; task SR 1.0 vs 0.7 vs 1.7.
limits: Offline workflows can mislead when train and test task types differ (Amazon shopping vs Amazon careers example). Task SR is tiny in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: Workflows learned offline on one class can be wrong for a neighbour class; build the store from the live class and gate reuse.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Prompting the model to recall relevant solved problems before solving (self-generated exemplars) beats 0-shot CoT and 3-shot CoT, across math, code and BIG-Bench.
numbers: Evaluated GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 (plus text-davinci models). Outperformed 0-shot CoT and few-shot CoT; self-generated knowledge added more on Codeforces. Exact table values not recorded here (e.g. a MATH row read 8%/24% Acc@1/Acc@10 for 0-shot, 11%/27% for 3-shot CoT).
limits: Needs a large enough model; with small models retrieved exemplars did relatively better; relevance of recalled problems is not checked by code.
agent_relevance: Source analogy is a transfer mechanism run inside the prompt. Our agent can instead retrieve by class from a code-checked store, avoiding unverified self-generated analogies.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: A meta-buffer of high-level thought templates distilled from earlier problems is retrieved and instantiated per new problem. Template reuse beat multi-query prompting at lower cost.
numbers: Reported gains over prior SOTA prompting: +11% Game of 24, +20% Geometric Shapes, +51% Checkmate-in-One, at about 12% of the cost of multi-query methods. Buffer grows more templates for diverse sets (MGSM) than simple ones.
limits: Authors' own 10-task suite; templates are class-specific by design.
agent_relevance: Closest published match to class-keyed lessons: templates retrieved by problem class, instantiated on the new item.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Skill-it! A Data-Driven Skills Framework for Understanding and Training Language Models
finding: Defines a skill as a unit learnable from a data slice and builds a skills graph of prerequisites. Training on prerequisite skills first helps target skills; naive stratified sampling by skill does not.
numbers: Stratified sampling on skills lowered validation loss per skill by only 0.007 over random in one setting; Skill-it gave a 35.8 point accuracy gain over random selection on the synthetic LEGO continual-pretraining task.
limits: 125M and 1.3B models; mostly synthetic data; training-time, not prompt-time.
agent_relevance: Which skills help which others can be measured as a graph; supports an explicit per-class dependency record rather than assuming sharing.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
finding: A growing library of verified, reusable code skills lets the agent solve unseen tasks in a fresh Minecraft world where agents without the library fail.
numbers: Zero-shot test in a new world on unseen tasks: ReAct and Reflexion made no meaningful progress; Voyager and AutoGPT (given Voyager's library) could. GPT-4 yielded 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5 in exploration.
limits: Minecraft only; skills are code verified by the environment, which is why reuse is safe.
agent_relevance: The skill library is a code-checked, composable lesson store; verification before storing is what makes transfer work.

source: Tang et al. (2025) AgentKB: Leveraging Cross-Domain Experience for Agentic Problem Solving
finding: Cited by ReasoningBank as prior work on sharing experience across domains for agents.
numbers: Not read; numbers unknown.
limits: Seen only as a citation in 2509.25140.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a follow-up read on cross-domain lesson sharing.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Cited by the CoT-mirage paper: reasoning models degrade as problem complexity rises beyond what they were trained on.
numbers: Not read; numbers unknown.
limits: Seen only as a citation in 2508.01191.
agent_relevance: Complexity is another transfer axis; read before final claims.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Can In-Context Learning Really Generalize to Out-of-Distribution Tasks?
finding: Cited by the CoT-mirage paper as related work on in-context learning failing out of distribution.
numbers: Not read; numbers unknown.
limits: Seen only as a citation in 2508.01191.
agent_relevance: Would test whether in-context lessons transfer to a new class.

source: Deng et al. (2023) Mind2Web and Zhou et al. (2024) WebArena (benchmarks, via AWM and ReasoningBank)
finding: Benchmarks used by AWM and ReasoningBank to define cross-task, cross-website and cross-domain splits: a ready-made transfer ladder.
numbers: Not read directly; split definitions taken from the two agent papers.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Reuse the three-level split (task, site, domain) as the design for our own class-transfer test.

source: Synthesis across opened LLM studies (2023-2026)
finding: Models carry procedures only partly. Failure grows along these axes: surface values (GSM-Symbolic), irrelevant content (GSM-IC, NoOp), premise order, task familiarity (Embers, counterfactuals), distribution gap (CoT mirage). Training method and data diversity change transfer (RL > SFT; multi-domain > math-only). Curated memory helps inside a class and its gain shrinks or reverses across classes for weak or offline-built stores.
numbers: GSM-NoOp up to -65%; premise order -20 to -40+ points; counterfactual tasks lower; RL +24.0 vs SFT on non-reasoning average; DC 23.3 to 50.0 on AIME24.
limits: Different models, years and metrics; not pooled statistically. Human data come from other angles of this subfield.
agent_relevance: Design rule: key lessons by problem class and surface-independent structure; test each lesson on a held-out neighbour class before sharing it; canonicalise order and strip irrelevant facts in code before the model solves.

source: Cross-paper comparison: which scaffolds changed results
finding: Scaffolds that moved results: ignore-irrelevant instruction plus distractor exemplars (GSM-IC), least-to-most decomposition (GSM-IC), self-generated analogies (above 0-shot and 3-shot CoT), zero-shot CoT (eases but does not close the counterfactual gap), curated cheatsheet memory (+9.1 GPQA). Did not rescue: changing the 8-shot examples on NoOp; Dynamic Cheatsheet on small models.
numbers: LTM about 2x CoT macro accuracy (GSM-IC, code-davinci-002); DC GPQA 59.6 to 68.7.
limits: Compared across different papers and models; not head to head.
agent_relevance: Prefer decomposition and structure-first scaffolds; do not rely on few-shot examples to fix distractor failures.

source: Cross-paper link: pretraining familiarity and transfer (Wu 2024, McCoy 2023)
finding: Both papers find performance on a rare variant of the same abstract task tracks how common the default variant is in training text. This is an LLM form of far transfer failing when surface form is unfamiliar.
numbers: Embers: 97% vs 53% (word reversal, high vs low probability output). Counterfactuals: lower than default across the task pairs for GPT-4 0-shot CoT.
limits: Correlational; pretraining data not visible.
agent_relevance: If our agent meets a rare-form task, expect weaker results and lean on code checks instead of model confidence.

source: Cross-paper link: SFT and distribution (Zhao 2026, Huan 2025)
finding: CoT-mirage: a small amount of in-distribution SFT on a new task restores performance. Huan: SFT on math teacher traces damages non-reasoning tasks. Both agree what is learned is tied to the training distribution and a small mismatch matters.
numbers: Zhao: 0.01% to 0% exact match under shift; Huan: IFEval 69.2 to 42.3 after SFT-think.
limits: One is synthetic, one is real; they test different things.
agent_relevance: A scaffold with no weight change avoids distribution drift but has no learned transfer, so the memory must supply class-specific help.
